### 2026-10-21 – # Oct 20: Project setup, RP2040 footprint and schematic work

**4.5h**

# Oct 20: Project setup, RP2040 footprint and schematic work

As the week is focused around music and making my own instrument, I decided to make a stylus synthesizer (similar to the Stylophone (see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stylophone)). My version will have exposed copper pads, which one can play with a probe (such as the one from a multimeter). An RP2040-Zero will generate the waveform, which goes through an analog circuit into a small amplifier and a headphone jack, so you can hear your music.

I was thinking about ways to make the project a bit more unique, and found something called Vactrol (see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resistive_opto-isolator). It is effectively a sealed photoresistor and an LED. When we play a note (by using the stylus), the LED should light up and the sound should open, whereas lifting the stylus will cause the note to gradually fade out as the LED gets darker and the photoresistor recovers, and shouldn't cut off. After I've had budgeting issues with my first project, I've decided to properly plan out my project before I begin wiring and gather a list of components, so when I opened KiCad, I pretty much knew what I was going to be using.

The first and likely today's biggest challenge came in making the footprint for the RP2040-Zero, as it wasn't included in KiCad's default libraries. To add to the confusion, my local electronics shop sold the RP2040-Zero under CREATALL (https://www.gme.cz/v/1518920/creatall-rp2040-zero-vyvojovy-modul-dual-core-cortex-m0-2-mb-flash), but the photo showed an ordinary RP2040-Zero, and the datasheet confirmed it, so I worked with the standard spacings and pin layout.

I decided to make the pads 1.8mm (a little bigger than usual) to make hand-soldering easier, since I feel like I will greatly struggle with the SMD on my first project. I placed all 18 pads of the footprint and drew the outline of the module.

![Designed footprint](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/bdcd7b912f8bf22bddfcf7ad574d86c4ae361544db61dceee15b1580977236c4.png)

Next came drawing the symbol. It was also a little tricky, as I accidentally misplaced the pins (they pointed inwards), so I had to move them and widen the body. I also named each pin accordingly (analog pins and power pins).

![Designed symbol](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/594411f4a8456a7b3b0ec49426696b7145b8fe31b966e2f0268619bea07b0d6d.png)

Then I wanted to make the schematic for the keyboard itself (the pads). This part wasn't so easy as much as it was tedious. It is simply 21 resistors in a series, and under each pair there is one of 20 copper pads. Every pad has a different voltage (the higher you go in the series the higher the resistance meaning the voltage rises), so we can easily tell all 20 keys apart. I tried using KiCad's auto repeat tools but it didn't really work, so in the end I had to resort to manually duplicating the resistors, labels and wires.

![Resistor ladder](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/c67c17ee7d228c9efc81d4d52ab7c5f106bdeed61dfc69a78c4d0e73f2dbcf95.png)

Next, I wanted to start the actual audio path. The RP2040 will output a very fast PWM for audio, so to smoothen it into a real waveform, I used two low-pass stages (1 kiloohm resistor + 10 nanofarad capacitor each). Then I wanted to work on my favorite part, the vactrol. I decided to drive a green LED from the GP2 pin of the RP2040 through a 330 ohm resistor (coming out to around 3.6mA). The LED shines on a photoresistor, which alongside a 10nF cap creates a filter that opens and closes with light. However, I am a bit concerned it might work poorly or cause issues, so to be safe, I added a 3 pin jumper which can be used to bypass it when we get to building the PCB.

![Audio PWM, Vactrol and jumper pins](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/c66a2329bb61a15258ebaebbf8d99a82087ba0815aebacf9234cbd8db7a4d41c.png)

Lastly, I finished today's work with a bit of work on the volume control. The signal coming out of the RP2040 will sit around 1.65 volts instead of 0, so I remove the offset with a 10 microfarad capacitor. I also make the signal smaller for the amplifier with 2 100 kiloohm resistors, to make sure we don't run into distortions. Lastly, there is a 10 kiloohm potentiometer as the volume knob, which can be used to properly change volume.

![Full schematic progress](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/d6e079de00a6238421403a660c0af2a5be7bfbcd6cf8c5074f58e37d8926b53f.png)

**Next up:** Amplifier, headphone jack and speaker, controls

**tl;dr: Began building the stylus synth, made a custom RP2040-Zero footprint and symbol, drew the keyboard using resistors and the first half of the audio path including the vactrol.**

**Total time spent: ~4.5 hours**

### 2026-10-22 – # Oct 21: Amplifier, headphone jack, controls and simulations

**4h**

# Oct 21: Amplifier, headphone jack, controls and simulations

I began today's work with the amplifier. I went with the LM386 amp. When I leave the gain pins unconnected, the signal is amplified 20 times, which is roughly what I planned. To keep the power supply stable, I placed a 100 nanofarad and 220 microfarad capacitor between 5V and GND, as the speaker can pull a lot of current. I also added a 10 microfarad on the bypass pin to remove potential noise from the RP2040. I used the datasheet (https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/snas545d/snas545d.pdf) as a reference for the circuit, and also added a 10 ohm resistor with a 47 nanofarad capacitor to ground.

![LM386 Amplifier](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/1d4b6b5fb0c0fa8f047d7dfb542b56a0c5c36b04a1a2b2088afb2720894b7107.png)

Next, I wanted the headphone jack. When I plug in headphones, I obviously want the speaker to turn off automatically, so I needed a jack that could detect this. I looked at GM Electronic (Czech electronics retailer) and found one which sadly had no datasheet, so I wasn't sure about its pinout. Continuing the search, I found a jack which had a proper datasheet with dimensions and the pinout (https://www.gme.cz/v/1501907/st-214c-jack-35-stereo). Inside the jack, the tip contact touches a second one, until a plug is inserted and pushes it away. I decided to route the speaker through this contact. With the headphones unplugged, the speaker plays, and with them plugged in, it cuts off.

![Headphone jack and speaker](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/a8fba9d377019f8245bd70dce96714d3e74197a97e79668b2dc87a195fedb7be.png)

Then I wanted to work on the controls. I added another potentiometer for the decay of notes on one of the RP2040's analog pins and two buttons for switching the octave and waveform. After this, I cleaned the schematic up (annotated, marked unused pins, etc.) and ran ERC, which came back clean. With that, my schematic was done.

![Finished schematic](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/8a260d7cd7566d8e071bb5495e623ad56382ec343cedf6eeff2562c2cf6e1e21.png)

Given I cannot build the circuit yet, I wanted some other way to prove that my circuit would work. I decided to simulate the audio path in the online Falstad simulator (https://www.falstad.com/circuit/). I tried the PWM filter first, which showed that a 1kHz tone would pass without being touched significantly (3.277V out of 3.3V on the source), while a 60kHz square wave got cut all the way down to around 0.25V. For the volume section, I simulated that at full volume the amp would get around 0.16V, which means that even after 20 times gain, it should be outputtable by the LM386 on 5V. I took images of all my test cases and put them into images/ on the repo.

![PWM filter in Falstad](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/e278734b57063a350b110a27aa9e9e9d40edb4ea4656b4220d23f37089fda527.png)

I also tried simulating the vactrol circuit. Inside Falstad, I replaced the photoresistor with a normal resistor and switched values between 1k (where the LED inside the vactrol would be bright) to 500k (where the LED would be dark). At 1k ohms, the square wave is loud, at 10k it gets softer, at 100k its more quiet and at 500k its almost flat. Thats roughly what would happen as one lifts the stylus from the synth.

![Vactrol at 1k](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/3485912f65fec883d88911ea2f9d60ffe51207085eb93243c30cc049b7bd0329.png)

![Vactrol at 10k](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/357c34bc38f8be24d3f89cfce84bbce95c015673ae769df5e998ec49dd4d213e.png)

![Vactrol at 100k](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/a022b8f2080585ab4823f49ca6ee7548b13b5b3ad7ef5fa026be618d856fdfb7.png)

![Vactrol at 500k](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/efe9a221ea34d83d2c3c59123031379ce6a1a61d439ce436d0aafa7824d54ac1.png)

**Next up:** Footprints, board outline and placing on PCB

**tl;dr: Added the LM386 amplifier, headphone jack, controls, finished schematic, simulated the audio path including the vactrol in Falstad.**

**Total time spent: ~4 hours**

### 2026-10-22 – # Oct 22: Footprints and starting PCB work

**5h**

# Oct 22: Footprints and starting PCB work

Today, I could finally move away from the schematic and work on the real PCB. The first relatively simple but tedious step was assigning footprints to individual parts. Most parts were relatively standard (resistors, capacitors, LEDs, etc.)  and I only had to make sure they would match the sizes and pin spacings I would be buying at GM Electronic. Three parts didn't have a footprint that would be usable for me, so I had to make my own. The first was the keyboard itself, which was the easiest, as it was simply 20 copper pads spaced 4.5mm apart. The keyboard is 90mm long, and easily fits on our 100mm board. The layout is similar to a piano, where the leftmost pad plays the lowest note (pad 1).

![Keyboard footprint](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/b04c4514e5a78b153aabd5c1a6a43aeddcad9a9f7d3034f977878e74ef36d1be.png)

Next, I needed to remake the potentiometers. This was trickier, as GM didn't have a proper datasheet and only included relatively hard to read images (https://www.gme.cz/v/1494573/pc1621nk010-potenciometr). From what I could make out, the shaft of the potentiometer points sideways (parallel to the board), which means the knobs will stick out the back edge. I was extra careful with the pin order, as if I mirrored it, the knob would likely turn the other way.

![GME potentiometer image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/b477a31745f2e770a0aada0e69c8bb09d8bd27d3ef2506e2c5a5e45a91c3c5e6.png)

![My potentiometer footprint](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/e311f8b2eab1dfabada46fefb4425a6abdeec8ef31fd41235bdb90dac7848531.png)

Next up was the headphone jack. The [datasheet](https://img.gme.cz/files/eshop_data/eshop_data/10/809-160/dsh.809-160.1.pdf) showed the PCB layout from the bottom side, so I had to properly mirror it in KiCad.

![Jack footprint](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/38f8b4f199756744be947ba8ee3f211c45189fec32b44a6411969560478f1259.png)

Next was time for the PCB editor. I made a 100x100mm board outline and setup some design rules. I set wider traces for the power and speaker lines, as they carry more current than the rest.

I decided to put the keyboard in the front and all of the input in the back. I took some time to shuffle things around to keep paths as short as possible and tried to keep the stabilizing capacitors as close to the amplifier pins as possible.

![PCB placement](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/be59f489ee856d932cd7fc6592f868e43143a80ea6976be3b6c5c10abae40707.png)

Thankfully, there were some beautiful parts, and that was the keyboard and resistor chain. I placed all 21 resistors vertically spaced out 4.5mm and could easily connect each pair of resistors at the top or bottom in a neat and straight line. The trace on the pads could then very easily ascend up to connect to the resistors without need for difficult wiring.

![Routed resistors and pads](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/5ad45cef519fa1f0dee49da050d7b8d97ea373bad29ce2a780f8b1ce342592df.png)

![3D view](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/1311c67eb82559d5543ef8efaec8088e1f15da299ee99d9b8da6cb7e11ccebd2.png)

**Next up:** Finishing routing, ground pour, finalization of the PCB

**tl;dr: Assigned footprints, made my own footprints for the keyboard, potentiometers and headphone jack, did placement in PCB editor and began routing**

**Total time spent: ~5 hours**

### 2026-10-23 – # Oct 23: Routing, ground pour and Gerbers

**4h**

# Oct 23: Routing, ground pour and Gerbers

Today I worked on finishing the PCB. I started by routing the power sections of the board (5V for the amp and 3.3V for the keyboard) as they're the widest traces. Afterwards, I routed the audio traces.

My first attempt at routing the input into the amp went quite poorly, as it was too long around the board. The amplifier boosts everything on the input trace 20 times, which includes any noise that it picks up. So I rerouted it to go almost straight up. Routing the board was quite fun and easy, as unlike when I was building my Geiger (week 1 project), I already knew how to properly use multiple layers, and so I was able to easily make it so that traces didn't overlap.

![Routed board](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/747b1e20670ed62616a347306557969fdb0cbbd0481a39cf7e5eebc563830498.png)

After that, I made the ground pour to easily connect all the GND pads. After the ground pour was complete on both layers, I ran the Design Rules Checker and got no errors and no unconnected items. Hurray!

![Routed board with ground pour](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/46e4549a1fe1e7497e775087f241f70572ed559b3f47204f89d24b15eaa950e5.png)

Before exporting Gerbers, I decided to make the board a bit easier to understand by adding silkscreen note names under each key and some very simple documentation to the vactrol jumper and resistor chain for the keyboard.

![3D Render](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/64e4efcd0bab4af288d6500c57568bc9dbb71633e4816422c467ef63ddb736c0.png)

At the end, I was able to finally export Gerbers and drill files and I tried uploading them to JLCPCB to get a quote. 5 boards came out to around 4$ with shipping of around 11$, so the PCB comes out to about 15$, which is exactly what I planned.

![JLCPCB Quote](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/0e244d23f22db152d9f314030eaac2ff546f21e0dd907a820802519ebecbd909.png)

**Next up:** Firmware, maybe CAD and finishing documentation and BOM

**tl;dr: Finished routing the entire PCB, added the ground pour on both layers, cleaned up and documented with silkscreen, exported Gerbers and got a 15$ quote on JLCPCB.**

**Total time spent: ~4 hours**

### 2026-10-24 – # Oct 24: Firmware and BOM finalization

**2.5h**

# Oct 24: Firmware and BOM finalization

Today I mostly worked on the firmware. I decided to use CircuitPython, as the RP2040-Zero supports it nicely and has a built in synthio module for easy sound generation. That means I mostly had to program the inputs and tell synthio what to play.

The main loop reads the stylus via the GP26 pin. The ADC returns a number 0-65535 and since we have 21 resistors in the ladder (above the keyboard), dividing 65535/21 gives us the pad number. Each pad is a note from C4 to G5, and converting the note to a frequency is easy, assuming A4 = 440 Hz.

![Pad reading logic](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/6bbe3aeb363529dbc6b7caaea5327c2de68afa7138df087cfe724247ecdb984c.png)

When a pad of the synthesizer is touched, the firmware does a note and the LED in the vactrol turns fully on. Sliding to another pad without lifting the stylus only changes the frequency, so it is much smoother than if an entirely new note started. If the stylus is lifted, the LED fades and the vactrol makes the sound fade with the photoresistor.

![Note fading and switching logic](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/79785003160c46ea479eb847234652504532d2abcb052df0a1cd2edc326c1fc2.png)

The two buttons on the PCB switch the octave and the waveform. It was a bit tricky to make the waveforms, especially the triangle waveform I had to lookup online. Notes are also sent out over USB MIDI, so the synthesizer can work as a MIDI controller if you plug it into a computer.

![Waveforms](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/46e0d7022cc99a127cf0e9e20b94a23cff3f86ffff3a4e39eee9cfd9207e8bdd.png)

I also spent a while finalizing the part list and BOM. Looking at GM Electronic, I found a cheaper 220 microfarad capacitor from Jamicon and I picked a brighter LED for the vactrol circuit. The whole BOM ended up coming out to about 38$ with shipping, so I will be covering the difference from the tier 1 budget myself.

![Bill of materials](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/010991509e89fc43845ad6d2a4b28465a06da8fd7b313d66844fb4c5da22f2a9.png)

**Next up:** Build week!

**tl;dr: Wrote the firmware in CircuitPython, finalized the BOM and got the project ready for submission.**

**Total time spent: ~2.5 hours**
